title: Taking In The Whole Landscape - Treatment of Immigrants to the US
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing complexity and uncertainty in life, rather than retreating from challenges or difficulties. Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to cultivate compassion and awareness, particularly when faced with issues like immigration policy and social injustice, and to find freedom and unity by letting go of habitual ways of thinking and believing in separation. By doing so, we can transcend our fears and obstacles, including the fear of time itself, and co-create a world of strong love and freedom for all beings.

sentences.text: What an awesome assembly.
So many friends and relations.
So much support and love and the complications of relationships in one room.
And somehow we've made a commitment to each other to stay in this room for a week.
How is that even possible?
For 60-something people to hang around in the same room for a week in relative harmony and peace.
But I think for many of us our attention is in the room but also beyond the room, especially those of us who happen to be Americans.
I think many of us are quite upset actually about various things, and maybe especially about recent developments in immigration policy and practice.
This has been a difficult area for quite a while, and I think most of us go in and out of paying attention to it because it's so exhausting and overwhelming.
Much more so for the people who are directly in the middle of it than for us, but still it's exhausting for us too.
But just lately so many people seeking asylum in our country are being treated so harshly.
So I thought it would be a good idea for us to pause for a moment before we complete our entry into the room and consider the frightening reality of another room.
An old Walmart store in Texas full of immigrant children who have been taken from their families one way or the other. 1,500 boys from Mexico and Central America in a converted Walmart store.
And I actually choose to have some confidence that the adult workers there are in touch with their own humanity, are aware of what a crazy situation it is and are doing their best.
But setting that aside for a moment, the whole thing is like a scene from a really bad movie.
I've been in the movies a few times lately, so I've been thinking about that.
Like a bad movie in which the evil villain is trying his best to create the most suffering possible.

And the setup in the movie is that people travel difficult journeys through many, many hardships, like a heroic journey to a place they hope will be a place of safety and redemption, only to have the evil villain grab hold of them and take away their children and throw them in jail at the last minute.
But the problem is there's not a superhero to come and throw open the doors of these prisons and liberate and unite everybody as the music swells in the background.
And the thwarted villain is banished to another world.
And he shows up for about ten seconds at the end of the credits, so you know he'll be back in the sequel.
So it would be nice if that's what it was, but it's apparently not that.
Apparently it's much more real than that.
And I actually did look this up, maybe you are well aware of all this.
I wasn't so much.
I felt pulled back into this this last week.
So I looked up this shelter in the converted Walmart store outside of Brownsville, Texas.
And it's actually run by a nonprofit group, not by the government, a nonprofit group called Southwest Key Programs, contracting with the U.S.
Government's Office of Refugee Resettlement.
The O.R.R.
I never heard of that agency before.
On the 3rd of June, wondering what the heck is going on, a U.S.
Senator, Jeff Merkley from Oregon, made a surprise visit to this shelter.
And the organizers or their government sponsors, somebody, actually turned him away, refused to let him in.
But that apparently resulted in a chain of actions that led to the media being invited in the next day.
And so I read a CNN article about this place.
Although it is a giant warehouse, they've created partition walls so that the rooms feel like separate bedrooms.
Although they've had to put five cots instead of four as designed in each room, there are so many kids.
And they have classes and recreation time.
And they have at least a couple of TVs to watch the World Cup.
So it does seem that my hope was more or less true, at least the reality that was shown to the media that particular day, that the adults there are trying their best.
But how could this be true?
That we live in a world in which our country has put 1,500 kids into an old Walmart store, even if it's as good as it can be.
So the organizers of this machine, although we're getting the hang of it, it's pretty overwhelming to try to figure out what to do with 65 people.
Organize us, give us bedrooms and classrooms and a TV to watch the World Cup.
We forgot that part.
Sorry.
It would work too, because of time differences, the games are really early in the morning.
We'd be perfect.
Can't have a different game each morning.
But anyway, 65 of us is pretty challenging.
So to get from 65 to 1,500, you have to multiply this group by 23.
So imagine 23 such sesshin composed of boys under 18 who speak only Spanish, and maybe their native language, if that's not Spanish.
Oftentimes Spanish is these kids' second language.
So this is huge, really.
And so many huge things are happening.
It's hard to take any of it in.
It's really hard to take in that we live in a country in which our own government is being investigated for human rights abuses by the UN High Commission on Human Rights.
A lot of things are coming home.
And yet maybe there are heroes and superheroes in this story too.
On Thursday night, I heard a really impressive interview with the development director of a Seattle nonprofit called the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project.
The host on the KUOW public radio station asked her various questions, and they both were doing a nice job just having a straight interview, not railing or repining about things.
So the host asked something like, officials in the administration are expressing concern that immigrants are falsely representing themselves and gaming the system.
What's your response to that?
And I was so impressed with how she responded.
She was passionate, but she was grounded, calm, and clear and speaking from her own experience.
And this is someone whose daily work, I assume, involves all kinds of contact and organizing of many people, contacting really frightened people who've been locked up, who've been detained.
I was thinking how Orwellian it is to say detained.
That sounds like you're waiting at the coat check or something.
Something's about to happen, you're just briefly detained.
And actually they're jailed and imprisoned, and maybe so for a long time.

But anyway, the development director of this group, who's named Mary Colby Wolfe, instead said, calmly, with energy, and with some warmth, instead of saying, yeah, isn't this insane, what's with these maniacs in our government?
She didn't say that.
Instead she said something like, well, the people I'm talking to every day at the SeaTac Detention Center are telling us about the truly horrific violence they're fleeing in their home countries.
She gave some examples, which I won't repeat.
Really horrible.
They're telling us about how they're selling their homes and borrowing money from relatives to afford the journey to the U.S.
They're telling us about the hardships on that journey, which can take a year.
They're telling us about showing up at the border knowing that there's a good chance they'll be picked up by American agents and not knowing how much of a chance they actually have to receive asylum.
They're not coming here, she said, with a naive view that America will take everyone in and everything will be better.
They know how risky this is.
They know that they could be turned back.
I do not understand, she said, how anyone could believe that any person would risk all that without all of this being very true.
And I don't even know what they mean when they say gaming the system.
What does that actually mean?
These are desperate people.
And they need our help.
So I was pretty impressed by this.
So I went inside and after a certain amount of forgetting and remembering again, I got on the computer and sent a donation to this group.
I thought it was a reasonably generous donation.
I had little choices, so I picked one choice higher than I quite felt like at the moment.
But how do we know how much to give?
Okay.
Oh no, you're just scratching.
I thought someone couldn't hear.
How do we know how much to give?
So tricky.
We're so privileged that I did give.
And then almost immediately in the email, somehow, I received a thank you from them, signed by the woman I heard on the radio.
It was much more than a boilerplate thank you.
I was pretty impressed.
I want to share that with you.
Maria Colby Wolf of the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project wrote to me and probably other donors this week.
*The past week has been particularly difficult for the immigrant community and for all of us who care about the human rights of immigrants in the United States.
That's why I wanted to let you know how much your gift means to all of us here at NWIRP.
We are humbled and honored by the hundreds of community members who have taken action.
After learning of the new threats being levied against immigrants in this country, attorneys calling to offer legal aid, interpreters ready to translate.
And with your gift, you joined in to make clear that families deserve to stay together and that asylum seekers deserve safety.
Thank you.
Today, you have helped us raise nearly $100,000 in this last week on behalf of our clients.

With those additional resources, we've been able to hold dozens of intake interviews with people in the Federal Detention Center and do several group presentations informing even more about their legal rights and what the asylum process will entail.*
*All of the parents have now received information about where their children are being held and a phone number to reach them.
And thanks to your generosity, we were able to commit to representing any of these parents who ask for their services for no charge to them.
For some, this will be a multi-year process.
We promise to be with them every step of the way.
Today, we could not have done this without your help.
Your gift has made a difference.
We will continue to use it to fight for these detainees and others like them.
We are deeply grateful you have chosen to stand with us and the people we serve at this time.*
So maybe not quite like the superhero in the movies, but here's some superheroes for sure.
So there's a lot of fear, isn't there, in this world?
And there's a lot of love.
There's an amazing expression of love she told us about.
And you can imagine the hearts behind that kind of action.
And how helpful it is to be reminded that love is also very strong, also very determined.
And that we can all contribute to that love.
That we can all help to reduce suffering in an unjust world, and it's probably always been an unjust world in many ways.
But it does seem a good notch more unjust this last year and a half, doesn't it?
So I feel like my job giving the first talk, and thank you for listening and inviting me to give the talk, whether you're involved in that or not, I feel like my job ought to be welcoming all of us.
Not just to the event, but welcoming all of us into a kind of transition.
A transition into the space and possibility of life together in this way, life together in sesshin.
So why would I be bringing up this stuff?
Isn't that part of what we're trying to take a break from, retreat from?
We call this a retreat.
Well, I don't think it is a retreat, really.
I think it's more like a forward.
The only way forward is to turn towards all of it, to face it, whatever it is.
To acknowledge that this is going on, and that this is also part of the landscape.

Just as much as Chuckanut Mountain behind us, Lummi Island over there, just as much as the swallows skimming the lawns, the collared doves calling, just as much as Laura Fish's very reliable oatmeal and hard-boiled egg breakfast.
And in my understanding, my belief is that our way of practice is to include all of it, to take in the whole landscape, nothing left out, and that this is the only way forward.
And I believe that we have the capacity to trust the depth of our love to be able to enter that landscape fully, with our eyes open.
And of course, we need to be wise about how we approach all this and what our sources of information are.
We need to understand that we don't really know what's going on in the world, that we've constructed a world based on various things that we've taken in or have been offered to us.
We need to be wise about where we put our attention, what we focus on, what we learn.
Out of that wisdom, we're of course disconnecting this week, and I hope you're taking that opportunity 100% to really just be here this week.
Maybe Norman or I in the talks, if it's relevant, will include some detail from some of those other worlds, or not.
But let's turn off our little portals into that certain cast of the world for this week.
But this is not to retreat.
This is not to pull back.
This is just to have time and space to find our feet in the real landscape, to open up to what is.

And to do that right now, in the lives we actually have, with the bodies we actually have, with the minds and hearts we actually have, with all of our conditioning and baggage and confusion, and with all of our unbelievable and surprising potential to be bigger and more loving than we ever quite imagined.
And for sure, we do this during a difficult time.
But are there exactly easy times?
Is that true?

As you probably know, in addition to working with people in this context, I've been fortunate to also work with people in another context with similar kinds of practices and teachings, the world of mindfulness.
I teach workshops on stress reduction, and sometimes they have titles that sound like they're about something, like mindful communication or mindful leadership.
I made a new one called Mindfulness and Emotional Resilience.
Doesn't that sound good?
I'm really proud of that title.
I didn't think of it actually, but I'm proud of it.
But they're all really about the same stuff that we've been talking about in this talk so far.
They're about how we can really be in our life.
I wear a different costume, and I use different language, talking about stress reactivity and using our cognitive resources more wisely, and living our lives fully.
I guess that works both places.
I don't use words like awakening or Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, but these elements are always there in everything we do.
It's been so useful for me to see that these three elements of our awakened nature, the nature of our heart, are always there.
Buddha: our unbelievable potential for awakening.
Dharma: the practices and path, and fresh perspectives, new ways of seeing things.
And Sangha: the community of intention, the community of practice.
Even though I don't say those words or talk about those concepts too directly, the participants usually discover those.
One time I was doing my five-week class called Mindfulness for Healthcare Professionals.
It's not mindfulness in anything, it's just mindfulness.
You know, what they expect.

And on the last day, one of the women in the group, a clinical psychologist who leads a big practice, I'm sure very important in her field, is sitting on a cushion on the floor, looking around at everybody, her eyes a little misty, saying, "Wow, I feel so connected to everybody here.
It's weird because I never really got to know everybody, but we're just so all in this together, and it's just such a powerful feeling, so thank you for being part of that for me.
I hope I've been a part of that for you."
So, discovering Sangha.
I just nodded and smiled, and other people did too.
We didn't have to make a big deal about it, because it's the most natural thing in the world.
So I feel really lucky to get to work in these different arenas.
It's surprising to me to get to do that for my livelihood, unbelievable to me.
It makes me really happy, most of the time, when I'm not overwhelmed by it.
But if I think about it for a second, it's actually also pretty sad.
The only reason you need people running around teaching this stuff is because there's so much suffering.
In that context, I don't even say suffering, I usually say stress.
Same thing, though.
People, even people with all the advantages, great education, lots of material support, are so baffled and bamboozled by their lives, by this collective life.
I was just thinking, if we had a really truly healthy and supportive society and an education that educated the whole person, we wouldn't need any of this.
You'd be doing something else much more productive this week.
But it seems that we do need all this as a way to respond to suffering and stress.
I do work a lot with doctors, and I think there are some doctors in the room here today, so thank you for your work.
And I want to report that our highly trained doctors are really stressed out and they're burning out fast.
They're upset by many changes in the healthcare system, which they find increasingly corporate and impersonal.
They're upset by how little time they have with their patients, and they have to spend a lot of their time and resources figuring out the right diagnostic code and doing their record keeping.
Oftentimes I'll see them for a 6 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. class after they've been in clinic all day, and then after class they don't go home and relax with their families.
They go back to the office for another hour to finish their charting.
I hear a lot about EPIC, which is apparently the predominant medical record software program.
They hate it.

And of course this is a different sort of quality of suffering maybe, a different order of magnitude compared to somebody who's fearing for their life, stuck in a detention center at the border, losing their children.
But nonetheless this is suffering.
And these are the people we are trusting with our health and our lives.
So it would be good if they were well.
That would be good, if they themselves were well and nurtured as they try to help us be well and nurtured.

But it's a weird thing: they're smart, they're very well trained, they went into this with great intentions, but they're also tense, worried, harried, and pretty judgmental and grouchy at times about all kinds of things.
But just like us, they're very high functioning.

High functioning people who rely on this training and a certain kind of intelligence and a kind of chutzpah to get through the day, day after day, until one day they wake up and they can't take it anymore.
So they show up for class like that, a little bewildered actually.
Most of them don't have a clear idea of what's really the problem.
They have a cover story, they can talk about it, but I noticed early on that they didn't really seem to be that in touch with the actual feeling of suffering.
With their own internal landscape and how it relates to this external landscape when they're going on about how broken the system is.
Which I'm very careful not to dispute, what do I know about that?
Sometimes I would push on that and they'd push back pretty hard, so I stopped doing that.
After a little while I invented an exercise, which I thought we'd try.
It's the first noble truth exercise.
The first noble truth of knowing your suffering.
But it says you've got to know it, you've got to really know your suffering.
So we'll do a little meditation, and we already took care of that.
Maybe I'll read a poem or something and settle the space.
And then up on a whiteboard or something I'll write some words and short phrases that stand for different areas of suffering in our modern life.
My invitation to them is just to take in each of these words, phrases, pointers, and just breathe with it and see if that's an area of suffering for you right now.
See what comes up.
I asked them not to talk or describe it or figure it out, but just be with it.
So you'll have to imagine the whiteboard.
I think it's good to actually see these things because we're such literary people, but it doesn't fit this form.
See if any of these are areas of stress for you.
Physical pain or discomfort.
Just breathe with that.
Is that a challenge, a distraction, a source of dread or fear?
The kind of thing that's often hidden from others, right?
Physical pain and discomfort.
An area of stress.
How about emotional distress?
Being distracted by your emotions.
Too emotional, not emotional enough.
Clueless about emotions.
Is emotional distress a source of stress for you?
How about just persistent thoughts or worries?
Just being sucked into that cognitive space.
Losing track of what's going on.
Stressed out by your own thinking.
Persistent thoughts or worries.
How about time?
Time itself.
Having enough time, wasting time, using time wisely.
Wishing there were more time.
How about time?
How about sleep?
Getting enough sleep.
Sleeping at the right times, not the wrong times.
Not sleeping.
Sleeping to avoid things.
This may be an epidemic, actually.
Most of us aren't sleeping well enough.
Is that a source of stress for you?
And is it a source of stress now, as we change?
That's the other thing that's neat about this: we do change.
So sometimes something used to be a source of stress, and now it's not.
That's kind of nice, encouraging.
A few more.
How about we take the world of relationship and divide it into two big categories.
Firstly, intimate and family relationships.
Taking care of, maintaining those close, intimate relationships.
Is that a source of stress and suffering?
Challenge.
Which is not to say it's not also a source of joy.
We're just focusing on turning towards the suffering, right?
First noble truth.
And then beyond those relationships, what if we lump all other relationships together into our social world?
Many millions of kinds of friendships and little touches and answering all those darn emails and encounters on the street and in the store and so on and so forth.
The social world.
Is that a source of stress?
Like showing up for that.
How about roles?
The many different roles you have to play in life.
How many roles do you have?
You could list them off.
It would probably be a long list.
Father or mother, wife or husband.
All kinds of cousin and friend and coworker and employer and employee and so on and so forth.
And how about when you have to suddenly shift from one role to another?
Like when you least expected it.
The world has a way of demanding that of us, doesn't it?
We're comfortably in our favorite role and then something happens and we're forced into another role that we don't like.
That happens.
How about food?
Eating the right food, the wrong food.
Eating too much, eating too little.
Not noticing our food.
Maybe you wolf down that oatmeal breakfast without tasting a bite of it.
It happens.
Worried about something else.
Is food a source of stress?
How about money?
An abstract concept with a lot of teeth to it.
Managing your money, planning your money, using your money wisely, saving for the future.
We briefly had a major donor at Red Cedar Zen who told me about how having too much money is a source of stress.
That was interesting to find out.
Two more.
How about stuff?
This is like first world honesty.
Stuff.
Managing your stuff, storing your stuff, organizing your stuff, keeping your stuff working.
The suffering of when your stuff inevitably breaks and you want more stuff.
The storage unit industry suggests that stuff is a thing.
How about our changing bodies?
Apparently we're all aging.
Are the changes in your body a source of stress?
It's not like any of these are supposed to be or not supposed to be, but just, are they?
So anyway, we go through all this, and then I go around the group one more time, and I ask them to do some rating.
We collect a little data.
I ask them to tell me what the top first, second, and third areas of stress are for them right now.
And I put little ones and twos and threes on the board.
And we get this impressionistic sense of the stress profile of this particular group: where most of the ones are, and twos are, and threes are.
I deduce different colors, and it's kind of impressive and sort of frightening, actually.
So here's the interesting thing.
I've been doing this for some years, and usually money or work, I didn't mention work.
Work is usually up there.
Time and relationships get the most attention.
But in different kinds of mixes with different groups, it's always interesting.
But lately, the last couple of years, there's been a clear winner every time, and that winner is, in fact, time.
People are stressed by time, upset by time.
I thought about it some more, and I thought, well, what's really the relationship?
I think it's largely a kind of fear that many of us, maybe most of us, have: a fearful relationship, I'm getting the sense, with time itself.
The sense that time is out of control, rushing by, never enough of it, that we're using it poorly, we're undisciplined, other people are controlling it in a way that's not advantageous to us.
We're distracted by it or forget about it.
You sit down to do one thing, and three hours go by.
What happened to the time?
Where did the time go?
One time, collecting this data, one of the doctors, a pediatrician, I think, said, "Actually, time multiplies all the rest of them."
So I want to say time, but what that stands for is all of them.
So lately at Red Cedar we've been studying a wonderful new commentary on Dogen's great essay on time, Uji, "Being Time."
I just wanted to share a few passages, a few quotations from Uji, and a few thoughts inspired by this book.
I don't have time for a lot.
This book is by Shinchi Roberts.
Shinsu is a wonderful Soto Zen colleague of ours who lives outside of Santa Cruz, California.
She runs a small sangha with her partner, Daijaku Kintz.
It's neat: Daijaku is a great scholar of Buddhism, teaches at the graduate seminary and makes presentations at Buddhist study seminars and stuff like that.
So this is her partner, Shinsu, who seems to me, anyway, and I hope she wouldn't mind being described this way, very down to earth, ordinary in the best sense.
A great example of our everyday Zen idea, grounded everyday practice.
I think it probably took her a long time to put this book together.
It arose from a series of study groups and talks that she gave on the text, studying it herself and studying other parts of Dogen's essay collection, Shobogenzo.
She weaves other pieces of Dogen's into the book.
Anyway, a few of us have been studying this at Red Cedar, and it's been quite delightful, because people who felt quite intimidated by Dogen are suddenly seeing some light.
It's nice.
And they're admitting a little more thoroughly that they've been intimidated by Dogen than they ever have before, which is kind of interesting.
You're like, oh, poor old Dogen.
Poor old us.
So the essential point Dogen makes, as I'm sure you know already, but it's a matter of living into it, and somehow it's revealing itself a little more lately, is this: there is no time by itself.
There's no time outside of being.
And we are beings, some kind of something that does being, right?
Dogen, in his famous way of mixing up words and stuff, created a term for that: uji, meaning "being time," or "time beings."
And of course, our dear friend Ruth over here made great use of this in her wonderful novel, *A Tale for the Time Being*.
And so we spread, it has spread this all over the world somehow, which is great.
Who would have thought a book like that would go anywhere?
So two things about this and then we'll close.
I know it's getting to be a long talk, so thank you for your patience, and feel free to sit comfortably if that's possible.
One of the things Dogen points out in the text is how little we really understand about time and how little we even turn our attention toward the nature of time.
In my quotations of Dogen, I'm tweaking a little bit from the Waddell Abe translation that Shinchi uses in this great book.
So Dogen says something like:
*Although you never measure the length or the brevity of the 24 hours, you never look at their swiftness or slowness, you still call them 24 hours.
And as evidence of their coming and going is obvious, you do not come to doubt them.
And even if you do have doubts about time, that is not to say you know them.
Since a person's doubtings of the many things unknown to him or her are vague and indefinite, the course her doubtings take will not bring them to coincide with the present doubt.*
You got all that?
A, you don't pay much attention to time.
B, whenever you do, you just get more mixed up anyway.
So I hope you feel appropriately chastened.
We're freaked out by time, but we don't really look into it.

We focus on the objects and activities and things that are happening in our view, somehow surrounded by time or lost in time or messed up by time or pushed around by time, but we don't pay attention to time.

It's as if we're outside and the wind is blowing and we've dropped our papers, and we're jumping around trying to keep all our papers from blowing away without understanding that there's wind, completely baffled by our papers flying around.
I think he says it's a little bit like that.
And so you'd think he would next tell us what to do about this.
Of course, you'd think wrong.
Next he says, nonetheless, the doubts you have about time are, after all, none other than time.
So something happens here, a turning towards time, even if we don't understand it in that usual way of understanding.
But how do we practice with this?
What do we actually do?
Or how should we be?
Maybe doing is beside the point.
Shinshu is quite impressed with one instruction in Dogen's text, where he says something like:
*We set the self out in a ray and make the whole world.
We must see all of the things of the whole world as so many times.
These things don't get in each other's way, any more than the various times can get in each other's way.*
So somehow, an opening to how the world is created and seeing something of its nature.
This first phrase, "set the self out in a ray," "set the self out in a ray to make the whole world," is really curious to me.
I looked at other translations a little bit.
Kaz Tanahashi's version:
*The way the self arrays itself is the form of the entire world.
Seeing each thing in this entire world as a moment in time.*
And a wordier version from the Shasta Abbey folks:

*Since we human beings are continually arranging the bits and pieces of what we experience in order to fashion a whole universe, we must take care to look upon this welter of living beings and physical objects as sometime things.*
They're not real things, they're just sometime things.
So maybe in the end it's just hard to talk about time with language and concepts.
How do we open up and merge with this world of being and time?
How do we fully inhabit and take our place in the full landscape?
It's not just mountains and waters and birds and detention facilities, but also time itself, woven into the fabric.
And maybe Dogen seems to be telling us that once we really find this way, enter into this with our whole hearts, we'll recognize that nothing really obstructs anything.
We think things obstruct things.
We think so many things are in our way.
In that lovely little hymn we chanted this morning, we said that the perfection of wisdom, embodied as a bodhisattva, a female bodhisattva, happily, is not obstructed.
We chanted, do you remember this?
*The perfection of wisdom gives light.
Unstained, the entire world cannot stain her.
She is a source of light, and from everyone in the triple world she removes darkness.
The most excellent are her works.
She brings light, so that all fear and distress may be forsaken, and disperses the gloom and darkness of delusion.
Unstained, unstained, the entire world cannot stain her.*
So stained is another way of saying obstructed, bothered, messed up.
The nature of this perfect wisdom of the bodhisattvas can't be bothered, can't be stained, can't be blocked or obstructed.
Time can't get into time, just like time can't get in time's way, because we are time.
And then here's the extra sad and important part, I think.
If we're afraid of time, and we are time, we are afraid of ourself.
We're afraid of our own being.
We're afraid of our own nature.
So this is maybe why practice has some urgency.
We have various Zen poems exhorting us not to waste time, as if we knew what time is, or if time was something we could waste.
*She brings light, so that all fear and distress may be forsaken.
She brings light, so that all fear and distress may be forsaken, and disperses the gloom and darkness of delusion.*
This is such a hopeful vision.
